description: We’re a team of six students from UDEM with a strong interest in space and data analysis. Through “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!”, we aim to explore NASA data, uncover environmental trends, and turn our findings into meaningful insights while learning together.
summary: Trend Detectives helps people explore NASA climate data and answer four questions: what is changing, where, by how much, and how strong is the evidence? Our prototype combines temperature and precipitation time series, geographic visualizations, statistical trend estimates and an AI explanation assistant. Regional analyses cover three study boxes in Mexico from 1992 to 2024. The statistical pipeline accounts for the monthly seasonal cycle and ENSO, adjusts for multiple comparisons, and flags results that depend on the selected period or possible abrupt shifts. Users can compare up to three variables and inspect changes per decade alongside uncertainty. Our goal is to make climate evidence easier to explore without mistaking a rising chart for a confirmed long-term trend.
details:
Trend Detectives lets people compare NASA climate variables across three study boxes in Mexico. Users choose a period and up to three variables, then inspect maps, time series, estimated changes per decade and statistical evidence. The analysis covers 1992–2024 and does not represent all Mexican states.

We use NASA POWER temperature and corrected precipitation, plus GPCP precipitation and MERRA-2 RX5Day exported through NASA Giovanni. Monthly regression accounts for time, calendar seasonality and the Niño 3.4 index, with a parallel model excluding ENSO. An autoregressive sieve bootstrap-t with 4,999 replicates assesses uncertainty; Holm adjustment addresses multiple comparisons. Period sensitivity and possible abrupt shifts are flagged. Annual five-day rainfall maxima are derived separately from daily POWER data.

Statistical significance does not prove a stable gradual change or its cause. Inconclusive results do not prove that nothing is changing. Anthropic Claude explains the computed evidence; the statistical pipeline determines classifications. Neural-network forecasting experiments were evaluated against simpler historical baselines and are not guaranteed future forecasts.

The prototype uses Next.js, React, TypeScript and Python. Codex and Claude assisted with implementation, debugging, analysis development and documentation. Source data, metadata, methods and code are available at https://github.com/Tobeist/nsqk . The hosted site is being repaired, so the repository is the reliable public project link. The intended users are students, educators and climate-data explorers. This independent prototype has no official NASA endorsement.
